extracted.intended_audience: students and enthusiasts solving classical mathematical and mechanics exercises (19th-century style problems)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and present classical plane-geometry, statics/dynamics, and calculus problems by deriving equations, using moments/energy, geometric constructions, or coordinate/trig methods; include necessary approximations (small-angle) and checks for admissible roots in constrained optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conservation of vis viva (energy) for rotating systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the equation of vis viva to relate angular motion and radial motion of a mass on a spiral/rotating system (e.g. Z' Ayr 72. dr' etc. leading to MA;W'^+mV = Imgr + const.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the energy integral (vis viva), substitute ṙ = V where helpful, integrate or differentiate to obtain the differential equation for r(t), and use initial conditions to determine constants so as to deduce the form of the spiral and the time dependence. The proposer demonstrates converting the vis-viva integral into an ODE and solving (including trigonometric solution) to obtain r = a + (constant) sin(ωt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equate moments about the tipping axis to find overturn conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a body (e.g. a uniform cylinder on a rotating plane) will upset, take moments of the centrifugal forces about the potential pivot line (AP) and equate to the moment of the weight acting at the centre of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either perform the integral of elemental centrifugal force moments for the whole body or treat the resultant centrifugal force as acting through the centre of gravity (resultant = M ω^2 c) and take its moment about the pivot. Equate this to the weight's moment to obtain a criterion (e.g. expression relating diameter to height and accelerations). The text shows both the full integral approach and the shorter resultant/centroid method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve forces and take moments for equilibrium problems (beam/pulley examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve forces into vertical and horizontal components and take moments about a convenient point (often the contact point with wall or pivot) to obtain equilibrium relations (e.g. P sin(φ+θ) = W, Pa sin φ = ½ W a cos θ, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric relations to express lever arms (BC, AD, AC, etc.) in terms of given lengths and angles, combine moment equations with force-balance equations, eliminate intermediate unknowns (like the length k or BC) to arrive at the required expression (for instance, an expression for tan φ in terms of a, h, P, W, θ). The page demonstrates multiple equivalent ways (vertical resolution + moments; projecting resultant forces; geometric construction) to derive the same final formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: For small oscillations, linearize and use either energy (vis viva) or torque-inertia relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a body is displaced by a small angle (e.g. a circular plate suspended by three equal vertical strings), approximate trigonometric factors and linearize the restoring torque; then either use conservation of vis viva or set up the equation of motion using moment/inertia to obtain period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume small angles so that sin ≈ angle and use approximations for tensions' components; compute the resulting moment about the centre, equate to I·angular_acceleration (or integrate energy) to obtain simple harmonic motion and the oscillation period. Example: plate suspended by three equal strings leads to period equal to that of a simple pendulum of length half the string (with stated assumptions about neglecting string weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coordinate/trigonometric identities and right-triangle geometry to relate distances and angles
rubrics_metrics.description: For geometric/trig problems (e.g. visible horizon from a mountain), construct right triangles, identify equal or complementary angles, and apply relationships like cosec, cot, and trigonometric addition/subtraction to derive formulae (e.g. d = A cot(α/2), D + h = A cot^2(α/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple equivalent derivations are acceptable: pure Euclidean right-triangle angle-chasing; using trig identities (cosec/cot relations); or expressing via sums/differences of cot/cosec. The page offers three different derivations illustrating this flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrained optimization: substitute to satisfy constraint, reduce to single variable, differentiate and analyze roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a function with variables subject to a condition, perform substitutions that satisfy the constraint to reduce the problem to a one-variable extremum; set derivative to zero, classify roots with second-derivative/sign theory and check admissibility under sign/positivity conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: choose parametrization 2h = a(1−wz), 2k = β(1−vz) to satisfy mna(a−2h)−β(β−2k)=0, reduce U to a function of z, set dU/dz = 0, solve for z, use theory of equations to decide which root yields a maximum given positivity constraints. Discuss boundary/parameter cases where only maxima occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction via orthogonal projections, rotations and cone intersections for equal-angle line problems
rubrics_metrics.description: To draw lines from two given points meeting a given line so that they make equal angles (or maximize mutual angle), construct perpendiculars from the points to the given line, rotate the plane about the line until one perpendicular comes into the other's plane, and exploit the right-cone locus or reflect a perpendicular segment to find the required intersection point P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction: from A and B drop AC and BD perpendicular to CD; in the plane ACD construct B'D (a reflected copy of BD) on the opposite side; join A to B' and intersect CD at P; then AP and BP make equal angles with opposite parts of CD. For maximizing the mutual angle, set up distances AP', BP' as functions of a parameter and minimize the cosine (or maximize angle) via differentiation; solve resulting algebraic equation for parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial upper-bound via pair-to-triad counting for maximum collinear triples
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper bound the maximum number of 3-point collinear ranges among n points by counting unordered pairs: each collinear triple contributes 3 distinct pairs, so the number of possible distinct collinear triples ≤ number_of_pairs/3. For n=15 this gives maximum 35; additional geometric constraints reduce achievable number to 26 with constructive configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives a constructive proof achieving 26 ranges using an arrangement derived from vertices associated to pairwise cone-vertices of spheres, then analyses which extra triads are geometrically incompatible (diagonals of quadrilaterals can't have a common intersection) and thus rejects certain triads to obtain the maximum achievable 26. Use projection arguments and quadrilateral/diagonal intersection constraints when constructing realizable examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: When cones/quadric asymptotic cones touch coordinate planes, require trace quadratics to be perfect squares
rubrics_metrics.description: For hyperboloids whose asymptotic cones touch three given planes (coordinate planes), write the general quadratic form for the cone and require that its traces on coordinate planes be complete squares; this imposes relations among coefficients (e.g. D = −BC, E = −AC, F = ±AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the coordinate planes as the given tangent planes and set up the general second-degree homogeneous equation for the cone; enforce that the planar traces reduce to squares to produce the necessary equalities among coefficients. Be mindful of sign choices and the interpretation (reject the sign that makes the cone a complete square if needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat resultant of distributed centrifugal forces as acting through the centre of gravity when convenient
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than integrating centrifugal moment contributions elementwise, observe that the resultant centrifugal force of the whole body is horizontal, passes through its centre of gravity, and equals M ω^2 c; take moments of this resultant about the tipping axis to obtain the same overturn criterion more succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shortcut is used explicitly in the cylinder-on-rotating-plane problem: compute resultant = M ω^2 c, then moment_about_AP = M ω^2 c · lever_arm, equate to weight moment, and solve. Use integral method only when you need distributional detail or to justify the shortcut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate sin and tan by small-angle values (sin≈tan≈angle) when geometric elevations are small compared to base lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: When elevations (e.g. rail cant h compared with separation a) are very small, take tan θ ≈ sin θ ≈ h/(2a) to simplify formulas (e.g. for equal rail load velocity formula), acknowledging the approximation's domain of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly notes that since BC will be very small compared with AB, one may take tan θ = sin θ = h/2a to simplify expression (1) to v^2 = (g r h)/(2a) etc. State assumptions and expected error when using such approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple equivalent analytic methods (integral, resultant, coordinate) and check consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: For many problems (tipping cylinder, centroid of quadrilateral, beam equilibrium, plate oscillation), the page demonstrates two or more solution strategies (elemental integrals, resultant-of-distributed-forces, coordinate/trigonometric algebra, or geometric constructions); consistency across methods verifies results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, produce a short method (resultant/centroid or symmetry) and a long method (elementwise integral or coordinate expansion) to both check correctness and deepen understanding; the text often includes both and points out that the shorter method gives the same final expression as the laborious integral method.
